make amends.meaning: To do something good now to make up for a wrong thing you did before.

pick up the slack.meaning: To do the extra work that someone else is not doing.
pick up the slack.example: Mack says Ruby’s not picking up the slack after all.

back and forth.meaning: Moving one way and then the opposite way, again and again.
back and forth.example: They pass their green paper, dry as old leaves and smelling of a thousand hands, back and forth and back again.

come to think of it.meaning: Said when a new thought suddenly comes to you while you are talking.
come to think of it.example: Come to think of it, I suppose they have a point.

in charge.meaning: The person who controls a place or a group; in control of things.
in charge.example: When my father beat his chest, it was to say, Beware, listen, I am in charge.

get the hang of.meaning: To learn how to do something well after trying for a while.
get the hang of.example: I’m not sure I will ever get the hang of it.

give up.meaning: To stop trying; to admit that you cannot do it.
give up.example: He is so speedy, so wily, that mall workers long ago gave up trying to catch him.

go by.meaning: (Of time) to pass. “A day goes by” means a day passes.
go by.example: Lately, a day might go by without a single visitor.

thank goodness.meaning: Said when you feel happy and thankful that something bad did not happen.
thank goodness.example: “He seems to be calming down, thank goodness,” George says.

be my guest.meaning: Said to tell someone they are welcome to do or take something.

without fail.meaning: Always; every single time, with no exceptions.
without fail.example: She inspects George’s right shirt pocket for the treat he brings her every night without fail.

come up with.example: “Maybe I could come up with something that doesn't involve … you know, paint.”
come up with.meaning: to think of an idea or plan.

get together.meaning: To come together; to mix or join with each other.
get together.example: The page is striped with green, which is what happens when blue paint and yellow paint get together.

fight back.meaning: To fight against someone who is hurting you; to resist instead of giving in.

mess with.meaning: To bother, threaten, or cause trouble for someone.
mess with.example: “See why you don’t want to mess with me?” Mack says.

play it that way.meaning: To act in that unfriendly or tough manner. Often a warning or a challenge.
play it that way.example: “You want to play it that way?”

do it justice.meaning: To show how good or beautiful something really is. “No crayons could do it justice” means no drawing could show its real beauty.
do it justice.example: I was born in a place humans call central Africa, in a dense rain forest so beautiful, no crayons could ever do it justice.

call it a day.meaning: To stop working for the day; to decide you have done enough.
call it a day.example: “Mack,” he yells, “maybe you should call it a day.

keep a low profile.meaning: To try not to be noticed; to stay quiet and out of sight.
keep a low profile.example: He prefers to keep a low profile around Mack.

get one's hopes up.meaning: To start hoping strongly that something good will happen. Often followed by disappointment.
get one's hopes up.example: I’ve learned not to get my hopes up.

in the nick of time.meaning: Just in time; at the last possible moment before it is too late.
in the nick of time.example: She leaps aside just in the nick of time.

hand over fist.meaning: Quickly and in large amounts. “Losing money hand over fist” means losing a lot of money fast.
hand over fist.example: He says we are losing money hand over fist.

go bust.meaning: (Of a business) to fail and lose all its money.
go bust.example: Only had her a month before they went bust.

command respect.meaning: To earn people’s deep respect because of who you are or what you do.
command respect.example: Even as I tell her this, I wonder if I can ever command their respect.

come to.meaning: To wake up and become conscious again after being unconscious.

put under.meaning: To make someone unconscious with medicine before an operation.
put under.example: “We’re going to need to put this one under,” he says.

green paper.meaning: Paper money; dollar bills. American bills are green.
green paper.example: They pass their green paper, dry as old leaves and smelling of a thousand hands, back and forth and back again.

the glass says.meaning: Said of the glass wall of Ivan’s cage. The wall seems to speak: it tells humans and animals that they are different and will always stay apart.
the glass says.example: The glass says you are this and we are that and that is how it will always be.

ruby sized.meaning: The size of Ruby, the baby elephant; very small.

beats me.meaning: I don’t know; I have no idea. A casual answer.
beats me.example: “Beats me what Ivan thinks he’s drawing.

get a clue.meaning: To finally start to understand what is happening around you.
get a clue.example: “Doggone it, get a clue, Ruby,” he mutters, but Ruby isn’t moving, and neither is Stella.

give the benefit of the doubt.meaning: To believe someone is good or honest even when you are not sure.
give the benefit of the doubt.example: I always try to give humans the benefit of the doubt.

big deal.meaning: Said when you think something is not important at all. Often sarcastic.

can't stand.meaning: To be unable to bear something; to dislike it very strongly.
can't stand.example: I don’t answer, so Bob licks my nose until I can’t stand it any longer.

can't help it.meaning: To be unable to stop yourself from doing something.

catch a glimpse of.meaning: To see something for just a very short moment.
catch a glimpse of.example: Sometimes, when we are lucky, we catch a glimpse of the moon through the skylight in the food court.

change is in the air.meaning: Things are about to become different; you can feel it coming.
change is in the air.example: Humans always smell odd when change is in the air.

doze off.meaning: To fall into a light sleep, often without meaning to.
doze off.example: Sometimes Julia dozes off, and sometimes she reads her books, but mostly she draws pictures and talks about her day.

dwell on.meaning: To keep thinking about something sad or unpleasant.
dwell on.example: I tried not to dwell on it.

earn your keep.meaning: To work hard enough to deserve the food and the place you are given.
earn your keep.example: “Time to earn your keep, Picasso,” he mutters.

every now and then.meaning: Sometimes, but not often; once in a while.
every now and then.example: But every now and then I see him sitting at Julia’s feet.

from time to time.meaning: Sometimes; not often, but again and again over time.
from time to time.example: Bob, who’s been known to munch on bugs from time to time, offers to eat him.

fall apart.meaning: To break into pieces; to fail completely.
fall apart.example: How to make a nest of branches (weave them tightly or they will fall apart in the middle of the night).

fighting words.meaning: Words that sound like a threat or a challenge to fight.
fighting words.example: They hear fighting words on the wind, when all I’m thinking is how the late-day sun reminds me of a ripe nectarine.

for fear of.meaning: Because you are afraid that something bad will happen.
for fear of.example: I didn’t move all night, for fear of waking Bob.

from far and wide.meaning: From many different places, both near and far.
from far and wide.example: People came from far and wide to have their pictures taken with me.

get by.meaning: To manage to live or deal with life, even when it is not easy.
get by.example: Gorillas get by just fine without learning how to spell.

get rid of.meaning: To remove or throw away something you do not want.
get rid of.example: That means he is the sheriff and he will be getting rid of all the bad guys.

go to one's head.meaning: (Of praise or success) to make someone too proud; to make them think too highly of themselves.
go to one's head.example: Bob says don’t let it go to my head.

going nowhere.meaning: Not making any progress; moving but getting nothing done.
going nowhere.example: I watch Ruby plod around the ring in endless circles, going nowhere.

have a lot in common.meaning: To share many of the same interests, feelings, or qualities.
have a lot in common.example: She and I have a lot in common.

have a point.meaning: To say something true or reasonable; to be right about something.
have a point.example: Come to think of it, I suppose they have a point.

have to do with.meaning: To be about something, or connected with it.
have to do with.example: “It has to do with the billboard.”

hear from.meaning: To get news or a message from someone.
hear from.example: Bob heard from a rat, a reliable sort, that they tossed Stella’s body into a garbage truck.

hungry for.meaning: Wanting something very much. Not only about food.
hungry for.example: At night, lying alone in my Pooh pajamas, I felt hungry for the skilled touch of a grooming friend, for the cheerful grunts of a play fight, for the easy safety of my nearby troop, foraging through shadows.

in a row.meaning: One after another, with nothing different in between.
in a row.example: I eat three banana peels in a row.

in the flesh.meaning: In person; really here, not just in a picture or a story.

keep an eye on.meaning: To watch something or someone carefully.

keep in line.meaning: To make people behave well and follow the rules.
keep in line.example: But my father knew how to keep us in line with a simple scowl.

keep at it.meaning: To keep working hard at something without giving up.

keep someone company.meaning: To stay with someone so that they are not alone.
keep someone company.example: I try to recall other keepers I have known—the humans who cleaned my domain and prepared my food and sometimes kept me company.

lag behind.meaning: To move more slowly than the others and fall behind them.
lag behind.example: When she went lame and lagged behind the other elephants, the circus sold her to Mack.

let alone.meaning: Used to say something is even less possible than what you just said. “A chimp could not write a letter, let alone a book” means a book is even more impossible.
let alone.example: As if a chimp could write a letter, let alone a book.

let down.meaning: To disappoint someone who trusted you.
let down.example: “It’s just you and Stella,” I say, and for some reason, I feel we have let her down.

let go.meaning: To stop holding something; to release it. “Let go of” a place or memory means to stop clinging to it.
let go.example: How to go vining from tree to tree (don’t let go).

look the part.meaning: To look like you belong in a certain role or place.
look the part.example: I used to be a wild gorilla, and I still look the part.

make a face.meaning: To twist your face into a funny, rude, or unhappy expression.

make one's way.meaning: To move slowly toward a place, with effort.
make one's way.example: Slowly Stella makes her way up the rest of the ramp.

might as well.meaning: Said when there is no better choice; you may as well just do it.
might as well.example: “Might as well stay one more night.

never mind.meaning: Said to tell someone to forget about it; it is not important.

no offense.meaning: Said before words that might hurt someone’s feelings: I do not mean to insult you.
no offense.example: “I mean, no offense to Ivan, but they’re just blobs.”

nook and cranny.meaning: Every small corner and hidden place.
nook and cranny.example: I’ve explored every nook and cranny of this place, except for a hill at the far end where workers have been repairing a wall.

not in a position to.meaning: Not able to do something because of your situation.
not in a position to.example: I’m not in a position to be picky.

on my word.meaning: A strong promise; said to show you swear something is true.
on my word.example: “I promise it on my word as a silverback.”

out of shape.meaning: Not fit or strong, because of too little exercise.
out of shape.example: I’m a little out of shape.

out of the corner of one's eye.meaning: Seeing something at the side of your vision, without turning to look straight at it.
out of the corner of one's eye.example: Out of the corner of my eye, I see someone running.
forms: out of the corner of my eye

over and over again.meaning: Again and again; many, many times.
over and over again.example: But even though I draw the same things over and over again, I never get bored with my art.

perk up.meaning: (Of ears) to rise and become alert; (of a person or animal) to become more lively and interested.
perk up.example: Bob’s ears perk up, although his eyes stay closed.

put into words.meaning: To express something in language; to say clearly what you feel or think.
put into words.example: It’s hard to put into words.

puzzle over.meaning: To think hard about something that confuses you.
puzzle over.example: I puzzle over why this would be a good idea.

stand watch.meaning: To stay awake and guard; to keep looking out for danger.
stand watch.example: He smelled the boy’s pain, and then he stood watch.

one's stomach drops.meaning: To suddenly feel afraid or sick with worry, as if your stomach fell down inside you.

sure enough.meaning: As expected; just as you thought it would be.
sure enough.example: But sure enough, he was a gorilla.

thanks for nothing.meaning: Said angrily when someone was no help at all. Sarcastic.
thanks for nothing.example: He says thanks for nothing, George.

that does it.meaning: Said when you have had enough and are now going to act.

think through.meaning: To consider something carefully, from all sides, before deciding.

thumb through.meaning: To look through pages quickly, moving them with your thumb.
thumb through.example: Julia thumbs through the towering stack of paintings.

tower over.meaning: To be much taller than someone, so you seem big next to them.

trail off.meaning: (Of a voice) to become quieter little by little and then stop.
trail off.example: “You’ll think of something,” Bob says confidently, his voice trailing off as his eyes close.

under one's breath.meaning: In a very quiet voice that others can barely hear.
under one's breath.example: Stella mutters something under her breath, a word she uses when she’s angry.

what the heck.meaning: Said to show surprise or annoyance; means “what on earth”.
what the heck.example: “What the heck is this?” he asks.

with room to spare.meaning: With extra space left over; more than enough room.
with room to spare.example: And there she is, so small she can fit underneath Stella with room to spare.

be a hit.meaning: To be very popular and loved by many people.
be a hit.example: He says, “Ivan, you’ve lost your magic, old guy. You used to be a hit.”

by nature.meaning: As part of what someone or something is naturally like.
by nature.example: Gorillas are not, by nature, pouters.

die in one's throat.meaning: (Of words) to stop before they come out of your mouth; to be left unsaid.
die in one's throat.example: Once again I consider lying, but when I look at Ruby, the half-formed words die in my throat.

cut back on.meaning: To use or spend less of something than before.
cut back on.example: He says he’s cutting back on our food.

day in and day out.meaning: Every single day, for a long time, without a break.
day in and day out.example: When I think about all the people who have taken care of me, mostly it’s Mack I recall, day in and day out, year after year after year.

all over again.meaning: Once more, from the very start; repeating everything.
all over again.example: You do it all over again.

as heck.meaning: Very; extremely. A casual, mild way to make a word stronger.
as heck.example: “I’ll tell you one thing, though: You’re sure as heck painting enough.”

could use.meaning: To need something. “I could use some advice” is a polite way to say “I need some advice.”

doggone it.meaning: A mild swear word said when you feel annoyed or angry.
doggone it.example: “Doggone it, get a clue, Ruby,” he mutters, but Ruby isn’t moving, and neither is Stella.

live off.meaning: To get your food or your living from something.
live off.example: He lives well off the ends of hot dogs he pulls from the trash.

wild cage.meaning: Stella’s words for a good zoo: a cage that still feels wild, with room to roam and kind humans who do not hurt animals.

watering hole.meaning: A pool where animals go to drink. For people, it means a bar: a place where people go to drink.
watering hole.example: At the end, the sheriff marries the woman who owns the saloon, which is a watering hole for humans but not horses.

be up to.meaning: To be doing something, often something secret or playful. “What are you up to?” means “What are you doing?”
be up to.example: “What are you two up to?” Stella asks, moaning as she tries to move her sore foot.

see past.meaning: To not be stopped or fooled by something; to look beyond what is on the surface.
see past.example: She’ll see past all of that.

come on down.meaning: Come here; come down and join us. A warm, friendly invitation.

die on someone.meaning: To die while someone is looking after you, so that they feel it happened because of them.
die on someone.example: “He says he’s not going to let her die on him, not after all the money he’s put into her.”

in its wake.meaning: Right behind something that has moved forward; following after it.
in its wake.example: When I dragged the crayon across the paper, it left a trail in its wake like a slithering blue snake.

come on.meaning: (of a TV show or ad) to begin to be shown; also said to urge a person or animal to move or act, like 'let's go!' or 'please!'.

get hopes up.example: I’ve learned not to get my hopes up.
get hopes up.meaning: to let yourself hope too much that something good will happen; 'don't get your hopes up' means do not hope too much, so you will not feel sad later.

make up.meaning: to invent something that is not true, like a story; 'a made-up story' is a story someone invented.

chest beat.meaning: When a gorilla hits its chest with its hands, to show strong feeling.
chest beat.example: And nobody could chest beat like my father.

claw stick.meaning: A stick with a sharp, claw-like end that trainers use to hurt and control elephants.
claw stick.example: If you do not, the claw-stick comes swinging.

paragraphs.context: In my size humans see a test of themselves.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Humans look at Ivan's big body and see a challenge to their courage. They imagine he is threatening them, but he is gentle and only thinking of sweet things.
paragraphs.simple: People see how big I am and think I want to fight them. They think they hear me saying angry, fighting words in the wind. But really I am just thinking about how the sun at the end of the day looks like a ripe, sweet fruit.

paragraphs.context: humans are always certain about things—that Jambo would crush the boy’s life from him
paragraphs.mainIdea: When the boy woke up, the watching humans were completely sure that Jambo the gorilla would kill him. (They were wrong — Jambo was gentle.)
paragraphs.simple: The boy woke up. The people watching shouted at him to stay still and not move. They were 100 percent sure — people are always 100 percent sure about things — that Jambo would kill the boy. They thought the big gorilla would squeeze the life out of him.

paragraphs.context: When I say the words, they surprise me.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan says out loud that Stella wants him to take care of Ruby. He did not plan to say it — the promise surprises even himself.
paragraphs.simple: I say the words, and I am surprised to hear them come out of my mouth. I tell Stella: you want me to look after Ruby. I promise to do it before she even asks me.

paragraphs.context: I can tell he wants her to see how much it can hurt.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack pokes Ruby with the claw-stick only lightly, but Ivan understands the real message: Mack wants Ruby to learn how much pain the tool could cause. It is a threat.
paragraphs.simple: Mack touches Ruby with the sharp point. He does not hurt her much. He just touches her a little. But I understand what he really wants. He wants her to see how much this tool can hurt. He wants her to be afraid of it.

paragraphs.context: It is the most beautiful mad I have ever heard.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ruby trumpets in anger at Mack, and Ivan finds the sound beautiful — he is proud that the baby elephant is finally fighting back.
paragraphs.simple: Ruby makes a loud, angry sound with her trunk. I have never heard anger sound so good. It is the best angry sound I have ever heard, because it means she is strong and she is fighting back.

paragraphs.context: But of course I know the answer. Nothing. Nothing will happen.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan asks himself what will happen if his plan fails. The terrible answer: nothing will change — Ruby will stay in the mall forever.
paragraphs.simple: I ask myself: what will happen if I fail? What if Julia never understands my paintings? But I already know the sad answer. Nothing will happen. Nothing will change. Ruby will stay here as the mall's star, and no one will save her.

paragraphs.context: I can’t let Ruby be another One and Only.
paragraphs.mainIdea: “The One and Only” means Ivan himself: the lonely gorilla with no family. He refuses to let Ruby grow up lonely the way he did.
paragraphs.simple: I am the One and Only Ivan — the only gorilla here, all alone, with no family. I cannot let Ruby become like me. I cannot let her be another lonely one and only.

paragraphs.context: She’s walking three extra dogs to cover my food.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bob explains his new life: Julia walks three extra dogs to earn money for his food, so he gets to stay with her family.
paragraphs.simple: George will not start his zoo job until next month. So he and Julia made a deal. Julia walks three more dogs, in addition to her own work, to earn money to pay for my food. And here is the funny part: all three dogs are poodles.

paragraphs.context: hunger, like food, comes in many shapes and colors
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan is not hungry for food. His hunger has many shapes: he is lonely, and he misses his gorilla family and the jungle.
paragraphs.simple: But hunger is like food -- it comes in many shapes and colors. At night, alone in my pajamas, I feel hungry, but not for food. I am hungry for the skilled touch of a grooming friend. I am hungry for the cheerful grunts of a play fight. I am hungry for the safe feeling of my troop near me, looking for food together in the dark shadows.

paragraphs.context: Like rotten meat, with a hint of papaya.
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is what humans smell like to Ivan when a big change is coming: like rotten meat with a little sweet papaya mixed in.
paragraphs.simple: Like rotten meat, with a little sweet papaya fruit smell mixed in. That is how humans smell to Ivan when a big change is in the air.

paragraphs.context: he wasn’t really such a sound sleeper after all
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan realizes his father was probably not really asleep all those times -- he was pretending, letting the children play.
paragraphs.simple: Now I understand something new. Perhaps my father was not really such a deep sleeper, after all. Perhaps he was only pretending to sleep, so we could keep playing.

paragraphs.context: something tighten in my chest, something dark and hot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan feels anger and grief as a tight, hot pain in his chest -- and finally stops calling his home a 'domain.'
paragraphs.simple: I feel something tighten in my chest. It feels dark and hot, like anger and sadness. I stop using the nice word 'domain' and call it a cage at last.

paragraphs.context: They toss them like banana peels and leave them to rot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan says humans talk too much and throw their words away like garbage -- but he adds, as a gorilla, that banana peels are actually the best part.
paragraphs.simple: People talk too much. They throw their words away like banana peels, and they leave them to rot. But everyone knows -- especially a gorilla -- that the peel is the best part of the banana.

paragraphs.context: I’m painting what I see in my head. Things that don’t exist.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan no longer paints real things like bananas. He paints the pictures in his head -- things that do not exist.
paragraphs.simple: My painting is different now. I do not paint what is in front of me -- a banana, an apple. I paint what I see in my head. I paint things that do not exist -- at least, not yet.

sentences.context: It would be easier to promise to stop eating, to stop breathing
sentences.simple: Keeping this promise is even harder than promising impossible things, like never eating or never breathing again.
sentences.grammar: An unfinished comparison: the second half ('than keeping this promise') is left out, and the examples are wild exaggerations to show how hard the promise is.

sentences.context: in a dense rain forest so beautiful, no crayons could ever do it justice
sentences.simple: I was born in central Africa, in a rain forest of amazing beauty. No drawing could ever show how beautiful it really was.
sentences.grammar: 'So beautiful' is followed by its result, with the word 'that' left out: so beautiful THAT no drawing could show it.

sentences.context: As if a chimp could write a letter, let alone a book.
sentences.simple: Ivan thinks George's idea is silly: of course a chimp could not write a letter — and writing a whole book is even more impossible.
sentences.grammar: 'As if' with past tense ('could write') shows Ivan thinks the idea is impossible and a bit silly; it is sarcasm, not a real guess.

sentences.context: Not if I can help it,
sentences.simple: I will not let it happen — not if there is anything I can do to stop it.
sentences.grammar: A short reply with most words left out. In full: 'I will not let [it happen], if I can do anything to stop it.'

sentences.context: examined the boy, as was his duty, while his troop watched
sentences.simple: Jambo the silverback checked the boy carefully, because as the leader of the group, that was his job.
sentences.grammar: 'As was his duty' leaves out the word 'it': as IT was his duty (to do).

sentences.context: Almost as if he believes I’m the silverback I’m pretending to be.
sentences.simple: The young gorilla almost seems to believe that I really am the strong leader I am acting like.
sentences.grammar: 'As if' paints an imagined picture (he does not really believe it); 'the silverback [that] I'm pretending to be' leaves out 'that'.

sentences.context: I like colorful tales with black beginnings and stormy middles and cloudless blue-sky endings
sentences.simple: I like exciting stories that start in a sad, dark way, have trouble in the middle, and end happily.
sentences.grammar: The colors stand for feelings: 'black' = sad, 'stormy' = full of trouble, 'blue-sky' = happy and clear.

sentences.context: As if a silverback could ever be cute.
sentences.simple: It is silly to think a silverback could ever be cute. Ivan is joking. Mack says Ivan is 'no longer cute,' but Ivan was never a cute little pet -- he is four hundred pounds of strong gorilla.
sentences.grammar: A short 'as if' sentence with the first words left out. In full: '[It is silly to think,] as if a silverback could ever be cute.' Ivan is making fun of Mack's words.

sentences.context: sends the whole jungle running, as if the sky has broken open
sentences.simple: A real chest beating is so loud and scary that every animal in the jungle runs away. It sounds as loud as the sky breaking open.
sentences.grammar: 'As if the sky has broken open' is a picture, not a fact. The sky does not really break. It only sounds that loud and terrible.

sentences.context: she is even older than I am and has eyes like black stars
sentences.simple: I believe Stella because she is older than I am. Her eyes shine like black stars, and she knows more than I will ever know. She is wise.
sentences.grammar: One long sentence gives Ivan's reasons for believing Stella: she is older, and she is wise. 'Eyes like black stars' is just a picture of her dark, shining eyes.

sentences.context: noble, contained, calm like a cobra is calm
sentences.simple: The bull elephant looks noble and calm, like a silverback. But a cobra also looks calm -- right before it attacks. The bull's calm is dangerous too.
sentences.grammar: 'Calm like a cobra is calm' is a warning, not praise. A cobra is still and quiet before it strikes. The bull looks peaceful, but he is not safe.

sentences.context: Of course, you also probably think we can’t walk upright
sentences.simple: You probably think gorillas cannot understand your words. And of course, you probably also think we cannot walk on two legs. You are wrong about both.
sentences.grammar: 'Of course' is sarcasm here -- Ivan does not agree with the humans. He is making fun of what they believe. Both ideas are wrong.

sentences.context: to recognize all those human sounds, to weave words into things
sentences.simple: It took me a long time to hear human sounds as real words. Slowly, I turned meaningless noise into words with meanings.
sentences.grammar: 'Weave words into things' is a picture. Like weaving threads into cloth, Ivan slowly wove sounds into words that mean something.

sentences.context: Gorillas are as patient as stones. Humans, not so much.
sentences.simple: Gorillas are as patient as stones -- very, very patient. Humans are not that patient.
sentences.grammar: 'Humans, not so much' leaves out the repeated words. In full: 'Humans are not so patient.'

sentences.context: Mostly I think about what is, not what could be.
sentences.simple: Mostly I think about the way things are now, not about the way things could be in the future.
sentences.grammar: 'What is' means the real world today. 'What could be' means imagined, better worlds. The two short phrases are opposites.

sentences.context: With enough time, you can get used to almost anything
sentences.simple: I wanted to tell the little boy not to feel so bad for me. If you live somewhere long enough, even a cage starts to feel normal.
sentences.grammar: The comfort is sad. Ivan says a cage can start to feel normal -- that is how many years he has lived in one.

sentences.context: the way they stare at me, sitting in my tiny box, just as strange
sentences.simple: Humans think it is strange to see a gorilla watching TV. But is it not just as strange that they stare at me while I sit in my tiny box?
sentences.grammar: A question that is really a statement. 'Isn't X just as strange?' means 'X is just as strange.' Ivan turns the judgment back on the humans.

sentences.context: it’s because I can’t talk back
sentences.simple: Maybe people talk to me because I cannot answer them. I can never reply, so whatever they tell me stays with me.
sentences.grammar: 'Talk back' here means 'answer' or 'reply' -- not 'be rude.' The second guess is the sadder one.

sentences.context: When I’m drawing a picture, I feel … quiet inside
sentences.simple: When I draw a picture, my mind becomes calm and still. I feel peaceful inside. All my worried thoughts stop.
sentences.grammar: 'Quiet inside' does not mean 'no noise.' It means his thoughts stop running. It is a feeling of peace, not of silence.

sentences.context: X’s marching across my wall like a parade of ugly insects
sentences.simple: I keep making X marks, one for each day, until there are 9,876 of them. They march across my wall like a line of ugly insects -- because every day in the cage feels ugly and never ends.
sentences.grammar: The X's are the days Ivan has lived with humans. 'Like a parade of ugly insects' is how those endless days feel to him: ugly, crawling, and never stopping.

sentences.context: the flicker of time it takes a snake’s tongue to taste the air
sentences.simple: A snake's tongue moves in and out very, very fast. In that tiny, tiny moment, the angry Ivan inside me could feel the wish for revenge.
sentences.grammar: Two pictures in one sentence. The snake's tongue means 'in an instant.' 'Taste revenge' means 'feel the wish to hurt back.' Neither is literal.

sentences.context: He doesn’t use it. He doesn’t have to.
sentences.simple: Mack carries the claw-stick all the time now. He never uses it. He does not need to -- just seeing the stick is enough to scare Ruby into obeying.
sentences.grammar: 'He doesn't have to [use it]' leaves out 'use it.' The threat alone does the work. Ruby obeys because she is afraid.

sentences.context: It’s not what I’m trying to create. It’s not what it’s meant to be.
sentences.simple: My painting is not what I want to make. It is not what I want it to be. It does not match the picture in my head.
sentences.grammar: 'It' is his painting, again and again. 'What it's meant to be' means what he wishes it were -- the true picture he cannot yet paint.

sentences.context: “I doubt that,” Bob says. “Smelly, yes. Stupid? Never.”
sentences.simple: I do not believe your plan is stupid. Yes, the paint smells bad. But stupid? No -- never.
sentences.grammar: Bob leaves out the repeated words. In full: '[Your plan is] smelly, yes. [Is it] stupid? Never [stupid].' 'Never' answers his own question.

sentences.context: He does not want to be a check mark
sentences.simple: Bob does not want the inspector to count him like one more thing on a list.
sentences.grammar: 'A check mark' is what the inspector draws on his paper for each thing he checks. Bob does not want to be just another mark -- he is a living dog, not an item.

sentences.context: It’s a new cage not unlike my old cage, except that it’s much cleaner
sentences.simple: It is a new cage, very much like my old cage -- only much cleaner.
sentences.grammar: 'Not unlike' is a double negative. It means 'like.' The new cage is like the old one, but cleaner.

sentences.context: They’re on the other side of the glass, watching me watching them
sentences.simple: They are behind the glass, looking at me, while I look at them. We are watching each other.
sentences.grammar: 'Watching me watching them' holds two watchings at once: they watch me, and I watch them. Both sides are looking.

sentences.context: she would have been through that door by now
sentences.simple: Ruby would want to know what is behind the door -- and she would already have walked through it by now.
sentences.grammar: 'Would have been through' talks about a past that did not happen. Ruby is not here, but if she were, she would already be on the other side. It shows Ruby is braver than Ivan.

sentences.context: I try to think past the babies and the motorbikes and the popcorn
sentences.simple: I try to push away my memories of human life -- the babies, the motorbikes, the popcorn -- and reach the older memories of being a real gorilla.
sentences.grammar: 'Think past' means to go beyond those memories, to look behind them. 'Past' here means 'beyond,' not 'the past.'

sentences.context: Gorillas aren’t chatty, like humans, prone to gossip and bad jokes
sentences.simple: Gorillas do not chatter. Humans do -- humans love gossip and bad jokes.
sentences.grammar: 'Prone to gossip and bad jokes' describes the humans, not the gorillas. The phrase sits next to 'humans,' and it belongs to them.

sentences.context: gazing at the iron bars surrounding her
sentences.simple: Stella looks at the iron bars of her cage as she speaks. 'I am not sure,' she says. 'I am not sure at all.'
sentences.grammar: The bars are her answer. Stella doubts she could protect anyone -- because in a cage, she could not even protect herself.

sentences.context: he’s not going to let her die on him, not after all the money
sentences.simple: Mack says he will not let Stella die while she belongs to him -- not after all the money he has spent on her.
sentences.grammar: 'Die on him' means 'die while she is his.' And the reason is money: Mack cares about what Stella cost him, not about Stella herself.

sentences.context: all the yogurt raisins in all the world for a heart made of ice
sentences.simple: Right now I wish I could feel nothing. I would give up everything I love -- even yogurt raisins -- to have a heart of ice that feels no pain.
sentences.grammar: A 'heart of ice' means a heart that feels nothing. Ivan wants that because Stella's death hurts too much to bear.

sentences.context: Is there anything sweeter than the touch of another
sentences.simple: Nothing is sweeter than the touch of another gorilla -- for example, when she pulls a dead bug out of your fur.
sentences.grammar: A question that expects the answer 'no.' It means: nothing is sweeter than this. Grooming is how gorillas show love.

sentences.context: This handprint can’t be so easily wiped away
sentences.simple: This painted handprint will stay. No one can wipe it away easily, the way someone wipes away the faint handprints visitors leave on my glass.
sentences.grammar: 'This handprint' is the red paint one Ivan just made. 'So easily' points back to the visitors' prints in the line before -- those get wiped off every night. His will last.

sentences.context: I too find it hard to believe there is a connection
sentences.simple: I also find it hard to believe that I am related -- across millions of years -- to humans, that rude and silly race.
sentences.grammar: 'I too' copies what humans say about apes. Ivan turns it around: HE can hardly believe HE is related to THEM. The 'ill-mannered clowns' are us -- the human readers.
